metadata.document_title: Clinical Guidance on Tuberculosis: Latent vs Active TB Disease, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Standard HRZE Pharmacotherapy

sections.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious bacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. It is transmitted person-to-person through airborne droplet nuclei generated when an individual with active pulmonary or laryngeal TB coughs, sneezes, speaks, or sings. A critical clinical distinction exists between Latent TB Infection (LTBI) and Active TB Disease: 1. Latent TB Infection: Patients are infected with M. tuberculosis but the bacteria are contained by the immune response. Individuals are asymptomatic, have normal chest radiographs, cannot transmit the bacteria to others, but exhibit a positive tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA); 2. Active TB Disease: The immune system fails to contain bacterial multiplication. Patients present with clinical symptoms, abnormal chest imaging (apical cavitary infiltrates), positive sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear or molecular GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing, and are infectious to close contacts.

sections.section_title: Classic Symptoms and Clinical Red Flags
sections.text: The classic presentation of active pulmonary tuberculosis includes: 1. Persistent, productive cough lasting for 3 or more weeks; 2. Hemoptysis (coughing up blood or blood-streaked sputum); 3. Unexplained constitutional symptoms: low-grade evening fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive unexplained weight loss, anorexia, and chronic fatigue; 4. Pleuritic chest pain. Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (occurring in approximately 15-20% of cases, more common in immunocompromised hosts) may involve lymph nodes (tuberculous lymphadenitis / scrofula), pleura, central nervous system (tuberculous meningitis), spine (Pott's disease), or kidneys.

The standard first-line curative pharmacotherapy for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis consists of a 6-month regimen divided into an initial intensive phase and a continuation phase: 1. Intensive Phase (2 months): Co-administration of four oral first-line antituberculosis agents: Isoniazid (H, 300 mg daily), Rifampin / Rifampicin (R, 600 mg daily), Pyrazinamide (Z, 1500-2000 mg daily based on weight), and Ethambutol (E, 1200-1600 mg daily based on weight) [HRZE regimen]; 2. Continuation Phase (4 months): Dual therapy with Isoniazid and Rifampin / Rifampicin (HR) administered for 4 additional months to eradicate dormant bacilli and prevent relapse. Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is recommended to ensure complete treatment adherence and prevent the emergence of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB).

sections.section_title: Adverse Drug Reactions and Safety Monitoring
sections.text: Baseline and periodic laboratory monitoring is essential during first-line anti-TB therapy: 1. Drug-Induced Liver Injury (Hepatotoxicity): Isoniazid, Rifampicin, and Pyrazinamide can each cause hepatic transaminase elevation; treatment should be withheld if serum aminotransferases (ALT/AST) exceed 5 times the upper limit of normal (or 3 times the upper limit with clinical jaundice or nausea); 2. Peripheral Neuropathy: Isoniazid impairs pyridoxine metabolism; Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6, 25-50 mg daily) must be co-prescribed to prevent peripheral neuropathy, particularly in diabetics, alcohol-dependent individuals, and pregnant women; 3. Optic Neuritis: Ethambutol can cause retrobulbar optic neuritis manifesting as decreased visual acuity or loss of red-green color discrimination; visual screening is required; 4. Secretory Discoloration: Patients must be counseled that Rifampicin causes harmless benign orange-red discoloration of body fluids (urine, sweat, tears).
